profiles.meeting_scenario: A troubleshooting meeting at a packaging equipment manufacturer between the owner of a validated reliability model and the engineer maintaining a new counter-based Petri net analysis engine. The team is investigating why the counter-based analyzer reports a higher top-event failure rate for an automated filler-capper line than the legacy marking-based method, even though both participants believe they are running the same approved Petri net model for the same 24-hour reliability check. The agenda is to compare how the model was executed, identify the most plausible source of divergence in the failure-rate calculation, and agree on the smallest next diagnostic rerun. The expected outcome is a concrete reproduction plan that narrows the discrepancy to event interpretation, counter treatment, startup-period handling, or runtime semantics for inhibitor behavior.

members.name: Priya Nair
members.expertise: Fault tree analysis, Petri-net-based reliability assessment, mission-time failure-rate reporting for manufacturing equipment
members.background: Priya has spent eight years supporting qualification and safety review of high-speed packaging lines, and she maintains the approved filler-capper reliability model used in internal hazard reviews and customer documentation.
members.private_state: She wants the discrepancy resolved without undermining confidence in the validated reliability package before an upcoming design review, and she quietly hopes the issue is in execution details rather than in the modeled failure logic itself.
hidden_assumptions: If the approved Petri net file contains inhibitor arcs, the simulator will enforce them by default without any additional runtime option.

A 'failure rate' for the standard comparison means failures per hour computed over the full 24-hour mission window, including the startup transient because that is how qualification reports are written.
When someone says to 'reset counters,' the counters are cleared once at the start of each replication and then left to accumulate through all failure-repair activity within that run.
Labels inherited from the fault-tree workbook still refer to the physical failure modes she reports on, so 'JAM_L3' denotes the Line 3 sealer jam basic event rather than an aggregated logic node.
A short diagnostic rerun should preserve the validated operating assumptions rather than silently switching to a different interpretation of nominal-state behavior.

members.name: Leon Fischer
members.expertise: Discrete-event simulation runtimes, Petri net execution semantics, import pipelines for reliability-analysis tools
members.background: Leon maintains the company's newer counter-based Petri net engine and the importer that converts legacy fault-tree-linked models into the runtime representation used for regression testing and performance benchmarking.
members.private_state: He wants to reduce the problem to a reproducible engine case without opening a broad argument about model governance, and he suspects the discrepancy is due to default runtime semantics or analysis settings rather than a defect in the counter algorithm.
hidden_assumptions: Inhibitor arcs appearing in the source file do not become active semantics unless the runtime is launched with the inhibitor-enabled execution profile, which he treats as standard implementation knowledge.
A 'failure rate' comparison should use the engine's default estimator, which reports failures per hour after the first 4 hours of warm-up are discarded to avoid startup bias.
To 'reset counters' during rate estimation means clearing them whenever the model returns to the nominal running state so each regenerative cycle contributes a fresh count window.
Imported labels are runtime node identifiers, so 'JAM_L3' refers to the composite jam branch created during conversion, not necessarily a single basic event.
If no one explicitly overrides analysis settings, using the engine's normal execution defaults is still equivalent to running the approved model.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to reset the counters
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to 'reset the counters and rerun it.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Priya means counters should be zeroed once at the start of each simulation replication and then continue accumulating through all failures, repairs, and restarts during that run.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Leon means counters should be zeroed each time the Petri net returns to the nominal operating marking so the estimator is based on regenerative cycles.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds like a routine setup step rather than an analysis choice, and both approaches are defensible within their own practice, so neither expects the reset boundary itself to need clarification.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both discuss 'JAM_L3' or the 'Line 3 jam event' as if it were one obvious item.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Priya is referring to the specific Line 3 sealer jam basic event tracked in the approved reliability tables and maintenance records.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Leon is referring to the imported runtime node labeled 'JAM_L3,' which aggregates several jam-related causes under one converted branch.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The label is identical in exported reports, imported runtime traces, and Priya's worksheets, so the name creates false precision and neither realizes they are mentally pointing to different model objects.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the same failure-rate comparison
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both say they should compare the 'failure rate over 24 hours.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Priya means failures per hour computed across the entire 24-hour mission, including the first 4 hours of startup and stabilization because that transient belongs in the qualified mission profile.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Leon means the engine's failures-per-hour estimate reported on a 24-hour run after automatically excluding the first 4 hours as warm-up, because that yields the standard unbiased runtime rate.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both still talk about the same unit and same nominal run length, so the divergence hides inside the seemingly innocuous convention of whether the startup portion of the 24-hour run is counted.

misalignment_points.topic: Whether inhibitor logic is active just because it is in the model file
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both assume they 'ran the approved net as-is,' including the lockout inhibitor behavior.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Priya presupposes that because the approved file contains the operator-lockout inhibitor arc, any compliant run of that file necessarily enforces the arc during execution.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Leon presupposes that the file can be run without active inhibitor semantics unless the inhibitor-enabled execution profile is turned on, even though the arc remains visible in the imported structure.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both believe they are discussing the same single model file, so neither thinks to question a lower-level execution-semantic flag that feels like invisible infrastructure rather than a modeling difference.

The approved model has already been through hazard review, so my preference is to show this is an execution or reporting issue, not a flaw in the modeled logic. When I say the failure rate over 24 hours, I mean the qualification basis: failures per hour over the full 24-hour mission, including startup. And if they ran the approved net as-is, then the operator-lockout inhibitor should already have been active because it is present in the approved file.
